The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding and Original Name (November 1931)
podcast.body: Opened in November 1931 in the St. John's Wood area of London, the studio was initially known as EMI Studios. "When it first opened in November 1931, it was known as EMI Studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding (1969) and Purpose
podcast.body: Sound City was built by the Sater family in Van Nuys, California, in 1969. Its establishment was part of a boom in studio construction aimed at meeting the increasing demands of rock and roll music. "It was built by the skater family in 1969 during a frenzy of studio building that took place to satisfy the demands of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Change to Abbey Road (1970)
podcast.body: The studio changed its name from EMI Studios to Abbey Road Studios in 1970. This change was prompted by the immense publicity generated by its most famous clients, The Beatles, who had released their album *Abbey Road* the previous year. "It stayed with the name EMI Studios until 1970, when the Beatles, their most famous clients, released an album called Abbey Road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Location and Construction (1974)
podcast.body: Le Studio was a purpose-built recording facility constructed in 1974 in Morin Heights, Quebec. Designers Andre Perry and Yale Brandeis envisioned it as a country retreat where the natural surroundings would inspire artists. "It was a purpose-built facility, built in 1974."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding and Location (1977)
podcast.body: The Power Station, located in New York at approximately 53rd and 10th, was founded in 1977 by Tony Bongiovi, the second cousin of John Bon Jovi. The building previously served as a Consolidated Edison power plant and later a TV studio for "Let's Make a Deal." "In 1977, the building was bought and rebuilt as a recording studio by Tony Bongeovi, the second cousin of some New Jersey kid named John Bongeovi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sale and Decline (1988)
podcast.body: Andre Perry and Yale Brandeis sold the facility in 1988, after which its condition and reputation deteriorated significantly. "Andre Perry and Yale Brandeis sold the facility in 1988, and after that it was, frankly, never the same."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Destruction by Hurricane Hugo (1989)
podcast.body: AIR Studios Montserrat was ultimately destroyed by Hurricane Hugo in 1989. This Category Five hurricane devastated Montserrat, leaving 11,000 of the 12,000 residents homeless, causing six-meter storm surges, mudslides, and widespread utility outages. While the buildings remained standing, nothing inside was salvageable. "But the bigger disaster was Hurricane Hugo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Tea Party Recording (1997)
podcast.body: The Tea Party recorded their fourth album, *Transmission*, at Le Studio in 1997. "The Tea Party, clients of the former La Studio and Moran Heights Quebec."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transformation into Trade School (Since 2004)
podcast.body: Since 2004, Metalworks has diversified its operations by becoming a trade school. It teaches a range of subjects from recording engineering to sound reinforcement and music industry law, with this educational venture subsidizing its recording business. "Since 2004, it's been a trade school, teaching everything from recording engineering to sound reinforcement to music industry law."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Equipment Trailer Fire (October 2009)
podcast.body: During a European tour in October 2009, the band experienced a disaster when their equipment trailer caught fire, destroying their gear. They stood by the roadside and listened as the harp strings snapped due to the heat. "In October 2009, there was a disaster when the band's gear was destroyed when their equipment trailer went up in flames during a European tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sale Threat (2010) and Preservation
podcast.body: In 2010, EMI Records' financial difficulties led to Abbey Road being put up for sale, sparking concerns that property developers might convert it into luxury condos. A "save Abbey Road" campaign was launched, and EMI ultimately retained ownership. "There was real concern about the fate of Abbey Road in 2010 when EMI ran into financial difficulties and the place was put up for sale."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Closure (May 2011) and Reasons
podcast.body: Sound City closed down permanently in May 2011. Its demise was attributed to the challenging economy, the evolving state of the music industry, and the significant expenses associated with upkeep, maintenance, and keeping pace with technological advancements. "The place was stripped of gear and it was shut down for good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Protected Status and Sale (2013)
podcast.body: Despite its abandonment, the Château was a protected site, which prevented developers from acquiring the land. In 2013, it was listed for sale at approximately $2 million, with an estimated half-million dollars needed for repairs to make it livable. "Fortunately, though, it was a protected site."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tax Sale and Restoration Attempt (2015)
podcast.body: In 2015, the town of Morin Heights put the studio up for sale for unpaid property taxes, briefly listing it for $18,000. A Quebec drummer, Richard Baxter, launched a crowdfunding campaign to purchase and restore it, but the current owner ultimately paid the taxes. The studio remains stripped of its gear and is slowly being reclaimed by nature. "In 2015, it was put up for sale again, but this time by the town of Moran Heights for unpaid property taxes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "France's Abbey Road"
podcast.body: The château earned the nickname "France's Abbey Road" due to its popularity and the high caliber of artists it attracted. "They called it France's Abbey Road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Abandonment and Deterioration
podcast.body: Following its sale, Le Studio was abandoned for years, remaining closed, unheated, and unpowered. Attempts to sell the property in 2008 failed, leading to its decay into a "wrecked hulk." "La Studio sat closed, unheated, unpowered, and abandoned for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Accessibility
podcast.body: Artists would fly into the neighboring island of Antigua and then take a smaller plane or boat to reach Montserrat and the studio. "Artists would fly into neighboring Antigua and then take a small plane or boat over to Montserrat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Appeal to Artists (Vintage Gear & Warmth)
podcast.body: Artists were drawn to Sound City primarily because of its vintage analog gear and the "warmth" that characterized the studio's sound. "Why? Well, a lot of it had to do with the vintage and lug gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barefoot Performances and Injuries
podcast.body: Florence Welch consistently performs barefoot on stage, a preference stemming from her lifelong enjoyment of dancing without shoes. This habit has led to several injuries, including a broken foot sustained from a stage dive during a Coachella gig in April 2015. "Florence, like Dolores Arreared into the cranberries, is one of those people who likes to perform barefoot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bathroom Audition for Manager Mayrid Nash
podcast.body: In late 2006, after many drinks at the Soho Review Bar in London, Florence cornered Mayrid Nash, a "seenster" and influential figure in the indie scene, in the women's bathroom. She drunkenly sang an Etta James song to Nash to prove her vocal prowess, an impromptu audition that led to Nash becoming her manager and securing her record deal. "Once she got Mayrid cornered in the Lou, she began singing an edit James song at her with the soul intent of proving that she had a big, strong voice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bipolar Grandmother and Childhood Trauma
podcast.body: Florence's grandmother, who was bipolar, committed suicide when Florence was 13 years old. This significant personal tragedy likely contributed to her emotional landscape and artistic perspective. "This would also be the time to mention that Florence had a bipolar grandmother who committed suicide. Florence was 13 at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Client Base Growth
podcast.body: After relocating to the Hamilton house, the studio's client base expanded significantly, attracting numerous Canadian artists like Martha and the Muffins, The Parachute Club, and Bruce Cockburn. "That's where their client base increased exponentially."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparisons to Kate Bush and Tori Amos
podcast.body: Upon the release of their debut album "Lungs," Florence + The Machine, particularly Florence Welch, immediately drew comparisons to artists like Kate Bush and Tori Amos, and these comparisons have continued. "Comparisons to Kate Bush and Tory Amos started immediately, and they continue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparisons to Other Artists
podcast.body: Upon their debut, Florence + The Machine immediately drew comparisons to Kate Bush and Tori Amos, comparisons that have continued throughout their career. "Comparisons to Kate Bush and Tory Amos started immediately, and they continue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Conversion to Residential Studio (1960s)
podcast.body: In the 1960s, composer Michel Magne purchased the château and transformed it into a recording studio. He converted one wing into one of the world's first residential recording studios, where artists could live and work on their projects. "He turned one wing into one of the first residential recording studios in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Current Facilities
podcast.body: The facility now boasts four state-of-the-art rooms for recording, one dedicated mastering room, and another specifically for video editing. "There are now four state of the art rooms for recording, one for mastering, and another dedicated to just video editing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Current Ownership
podcast.body: Upon Daniel Lanois' departure to work with U2, Bob Doige assumed ownership and continues to operate the studio today. "When that happened, a guy named Bob Doige took over the studio and runs it to this day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Current Status (Avatar Studios)
podcast.body: The Power Station continues to operate today under a new name, Avatar Studios. "The power station still exists, although it's not called that anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Grohl's Documentary and Preservation Efforts
podcast.body: After the studio's closure, Dave Grohl of the Foo Fighters purchased one of its famous mixing consoles for his private home studio. Motivated to preserve the memory of this "greatest unsung recording studio," he directed a documentary film titled *Sound City*, interviewing approximately 200 people. "So he directed a documentary called Sound City, which he says is a film about America's greatest unsung recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline Due to Label Resistance
podcast.body: One factor in the studio's decline was record labels' increasing dislike for artists working in such remote locations, making it difficult to monitor projects despite the labels' ability to recoup costs from future sales. "First record labels didn't like the fact that their artists were so far away working in places where they couldn't easily check up on them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline, Owner's Suicide, and Abandonment (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: The Château encountered legal problems in the mid-1980s, culminating in owner Michel Magne's suicide. The buildings were subsequently abandoned and began to fall into disrepair. "Sadly, the place ran into legal problems in the mid-80s, and owner Michelle Magne committed suicide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinctive Drum Sound
podcast.body: A key characteristic of recordings from The Power Station was its unique drum sound, described as "big, powerful and boomed." This was achieved through the studio's special ambient acoustics, sometimes augmented with noise gates on kits like Tony Thompson's. "The biggest difference between the power station and just about everywhere else was how drums sounded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dyspraxia Diagnosis and Self-Consciousness
podcast.body: While living in New York, Florence was diagnosed with dyspraxia, a genetic neurological condition affecting physical coordination, balance, and potentially social skills. This diagnosis, combined with being uprooted from the UK, being tall, and having bright red hair (dyed at age 10), made her feel "even more different" and very self-conscious, leading her to find escape in music. "This is a genetic neurological condition that makes it tough for someone to plan and coordinate their physical movements."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Artistic Inspiration
podcast.body: Florence's mother was a New York academic and a professor of Renaissance studies, which exposed Florence to a wealth of Renaissance material during her childhood. Her favorite painting was "Saint Agatha of Sicily" by Pierro de la Francesca (c. 1450), which depicts Agatha with her breasts cut off, reflecting an early inclination towards dark and evocative imagery. "Her mum is an academic from New York and is an actual professor of Renaissance studies. So you can imagine the kind of material that lay around the house as Florence was growing up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Singing at Funerals
podcast.body: At age 10 or 11, Florence's strong voice led her to become the "go-to person for singing at funerals," an experience that would have had a profound impact on her as a young child. "She had such a lovely voice that she became the go-to person for singing at funerals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Use and Genre Expansion
podcast.body: In its early years, EMI Studios was utilized for recording orchestras, film work, light popular music, and jazz. Rock music only became a significant part of its repertoire in the 1960s. "It was used for recording orchestras, film work, light-popping music, and jazz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Educational Initiative (Abbey Road Institute)
podcast.body: Abbey Road has established the Abbey Road Institute, an educational initiative headed by Luca Barassi. The institute aims to share the studio's over 80 years of expertise and knowledge through vocational training for aspiring music industry professionals. "This official name is Abbey Road Institute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution to Nimbus School of Recording & Media
podcast.body: The studio eventually faced challenges and evolved into the Nimbus School of Recording & Media. It is currently run by Garth Richardson, son of the renowned Canadian producer Jack Richardson, and co-owned by famous Canadian producer Bob Ezrin, known for his work on Pink Floyd's *The Wall* and numerous Kiss records. "Couldn't make it after a while, and eventually evolved into the nimbus school of recording in media, and is run by Garth Richardson, son of the famous Canadian producer Jack Richardson, and is co-owned by Bob Ezren, the famous Canadian producer of Pink Floyd's The Wall, and a ton of kiss records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Client List
podcast.body: Sound City hosted a wide range of influential artists, including Metallica, Johnny Cash, REO Speedwagon, Nine Inch Nails, Grateful Dead, Weezer, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Tool, Blind Melon, Slipknot, and Queens of the Stone Age. "Metallica, Johnny Cash, Ario Speedwagon, 9-inch nails, grateful dead, Weezer, Red O'Chillie Pepper's tool, Blind Melon, Slipknot, Queens of the Stone Age, they and dozens more use the studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Microphone Collection
podcast.body: One of the studio's highlights for clients is its exceptional collection of microphones, which includes rare and high-quality vintage mics dating back over 70 years. "And one of the things clients love about this place is the selection of microphones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Facilities and Gear
podcast.body: The complex now houses three studios, each equipped with state-of-the-art gear. Studio One is notable for its 72-channel mixing console. The facility also features an open-air courtyard with a small putting green. "The warehouse studio's complex now contains three studios, all containing state of the art gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family Background and Influences
podcast.body: Florence's father, Nick, was an "old punk" who had associations with Joe Strummer before The Clash formed, and later became an ad executive for Aero Chocolate Bars, resembling Andy Warhol. Her paternal grandfather hung out with the Warhol crowd at Studio 54, and another grandfather, a deputy editor of the Daily Telegraph, gave her the soundtrack to *The Rocky Horror Picture Show*, which became her first favorite record and sparked a crush on its creator, Richard O'Brien, at age 10. "And then there's her father, Nick. He was an old punk who once hung out with Joe Strummer in the days before he joined the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Client and Legendary Recordings
podcast.body: Neil Young was the first artist to use the studio, recording his *After the Gold Rush* album there. The studio subsequently became the site for numerous iconic albums, including Fleetwood Mac's *Rumours*, the debut album by Rage Against the Machine, and Tom Petty's *Damn the Torpedoes*. "And the first guy to use the place was Neil Young for his after the gold rush album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Florence Welch's Artistic and Academic Family Background
podcast.body: Florence Leontine Mary Welch comes from a highly artistic, literary, and academic family. Her father is an advertising executive who encouraged her to explore diverse music, moving beyond Ramones records. Her mother is a highly educated academic, holding positions at institutions like Harvard, Warburg, University of London, and King's College London, and is a professor of Renaissance studies, which informed Florence's artistic aesthetic. Her uncle is a renowned satirist, freelance journalist for British newspapers, broadcaster, and TV writer, while an aunt served as an editor of The Daily Telegraph. "Florence, Leontine, Mary Welch. Dad is an advertising executive who insisted that Florence put away the Ramones records and tried different music. Mom is an academic, Harvard, Warburg, University of London, King's College London. And she's a professor of Renaissance studies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding and Expansion
podcast.body: Metalworks first came online in 1978, established by the band Triumph in a non-descript industrial plaza in Mississauga, West of Toronto. Triumph built the studio to avoid the time pressures of recording in external facilities, and the complex expanded significantly over the years. "It first went online in 1978, when the band Triumph didn't want the time pressures of recording in someone else's studio, and over the years, the complex got bigger and bigger and bigger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding and Location
podcast.body: Grant Avenue Studios is located in the east end of Hamilton, in a house originally built in 1917. Brothers Daniel and Bob Lanois established the studio here after moving their recording operations from their mother's basement laundry room. "When two Hamilton brothers, Daniel and Bob Landwaw, decided to move the recording business out of their mother's basement, they were set up in the laundry room, they moved into the house."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding by George Martin (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: After establishing Associated Independent Recording (AIR) in London, producer George Martin and his wife, who were fond of Montserrat, built a state-of-the-art residential recording facility on the Caribbean island in the mid-1970s. "So in the mid-70s, they did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grade II Listed Building Status
podcast.body: The British government has designated Abbey Road a Grade II listed building, recognizing its special architectural or historical interest. This status requires special permission for any alterations and prohibits major structural changes, securing its future. "Meanwhile, the British government has declared Abbey Road to be a grade two listed building, which means it's a building of special architectural or historical interest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Haunted Reputation
podcast.body: During its operational years, the Château was said to be haunted, with guests reporting "weird apparitions and touches on the shoulder when no one was there." "Back in the day, though, the Château was said to be haunted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Background
podcast.body: Located in rural France, this was a French château built in 1740 on the remnants of a 16th-century structure. It featured two wings, 30 rooms, a swimming pool, a tennis court, outbuildings, and 42,000 acres of parkland. "It was an honest-to-god French château that was built in 1740 on the remains of an earlier building that dated back to sometime in the mid-16th century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Iconic Album Cover Location
podcast.body: The studio's entrance and the famous zebra crosswalk directly in front of it are prominently featured on the front cover of The Beatles' *Abbey Road* album, visible just above Paul McCartney's head. "Now, if you look at the front cover of that album, you can see the entrance to the studio just above Paul McCartney's head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Rock Recording
podcast.body: The Power Station's innovative acoustic approach gained immense popularity, profoundly changing rock recording techniques for years. It fostered a demand for bigger drum sounds, moving away from close-miking and instead leveraging natural room reverb found in large spaces. "The power station, the studio, their approach was so popular that it changed the way many rock recordings were made for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Innovative Reverberation Time-Based Design
podcast.body: Bongiovi designed The Power Station as a "reverberation time-based studio," incorporating a deliberate, slight reverb of about three-quarters of a second in the main recording room. This decay time matched that of the original Motown Studios in Detroit, resulting in records that sounded "live in full of energy." "Tony Bongeovi built the power station as a reverberation time-based studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: International Attention and Eno Collaboration
podcast.body: The studio gained international recognition, hosting clients such as Rick James and Talking Heads. This attracted Brian Eno to Hamilton, where he met Daniel Lanois. Lanois and Eno collaborated on several small projects before Eno invited Lanois to work on U2's *The Unforgettable Fire* album. "And this is how Brian Eno came to work in Hamilton where he met Daniel Landwaw."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Isolation and Inspiration for Artists
podcast.body: Artists highly valued the studio's isolated location, which allowed them to mingle with locals, immerse themselves in the atmosphere, and find unique inspiration unavailable elsewhere. "Artists loved it because it was so isolated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Lennon DNA Anecdote
podcast.body: An anecdote suggests that an ancient microphone in Studio Two could potentially reveal John Lennon's DNA if analyzed, highlighting its direct connection to legendary artists. "you know, if you analyze that one for DNA, you'd find a bunch of John Lennon in there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legacy and 606 Studios
podcast.body: Sound City's legacy continues through Dave Grohl's documentary and the physical relocation of its famous mixing console and other gear to 606 Studios, the Foo Fighters' recording fortress in Northridge, California. "A lot of the gear from Sound City, including its famous mixing console, was purchased by Dave Grohl and is now installed at 606 Studios, the Foo Fighters Recording Fortress in Northbridge, California."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Literary and Dark Interests
podcast.body: During her time at an exclusive private school, Florence developed a deep interest in literature, particularly Emily Dickinson and Emily Brontë. She also cultivated a fascination with Jack the Ripper and murder, with "the grizzlier, the better," indicating an early attraction to macabre themes. "She devoured all sorts of literature, especially Emily Dickinson and Emily Bronte. Oh, and she also developed a thing for anything to do with Jack the Ripper and anything to do with murder, the grizzlier, the better."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Location and Building History
podcast.body: The Warehouse Studio is situated in the Gastown area of Vancouver, operating out of the city's oldest brick building. Built in 1886 as a grocery warehouse, it later served as Vancouver City Hall, then reverted to a glass company warehouse. After falling into disuse and suffering fires, Bryan Adams purchased and extensively restored the almost completely burned-out building in 1991. "It was built, yes, as a warehouse, a grocery warehouse in 1886."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Low Sales for Combined CD/7-inch Single (64 copies)
podcast.body: A unique British release of Florence + The Machine's "Rabbit Heart" featured a CD single bundled with a 7-inch vinyl single of the same song. Despite this interesting physical package, it achieved very low commercial success, selling only 64 copies in the entire UK. "Yeah, it sold 64 copies in the entire UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 1: B-Sides and Bonus Tracks

podcast.title: Musical Legacy
podcast.body: Despite the physical destruction of the studio, the music created within its walls endures as its lasting legacy. "The only thing that survives was the music that was made there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Notable Clients
podcast.body: The studio has attracted a wide array of prominent artists from around the world, including The Offspring, Slayer, The Tragically Hip, Three Days Grace, Metallica, AC/DC, R.E.M., Matthew Good, Nickelback, and Muse (who recorded their 2015 album *Drones* there). "Warehouse studios has been very popular with some big names from all over the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Notable Clients and Albums
podcast.body: Over its decade of operation, AIR Montserrat hosted many major artists, including Bush, Elton John, Supertramp, The Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Duran Duran, Black Sabbath, Paul McCartney, and Dire Straits. Albums like *Brothers in Arms*, *Ghosts in the Machine*, and *Synchronicity* were recorded there. "Bush, Elton Johns, Super Tramp, The Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Durand Durand, Black Sabbath, Paul McCartney, Dire Straits, they all went to Air Studios Montserrat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Notable Clients and Recordings
podcast.body: Many famous artists recorded and performed at the Château. The Grateful Dead recorded there and played a show on its grounds. Elton John named his 1972 album after the place (the first of three he recorded there). Pink Floyd, T. Rex, David Bowie, Fleetwood Mac, and Iggy Pop (who recorded his 1977 album *The Idiot* with Bowie) also utilized the studio. "The Grateful Dad not only recorded there, but played a show on its grounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Over-production and Convergence of Female Artists
podcast.body: A point of concern regarding Florence + The Machine's album "High As Hope" is the extensive list of collaborators, with "Hunger" alone reportedly involving seven producers and four lyricists. This phenomenon is highlighted as a broader issue affecting many contemporary female artists like Sia, Adele, Lorde, Lady Gaga, and Lana Del Rey, who, by consistently employing the same professional lyricists and producers, are losing their initial distinctive styles and converging into a similar sound. "si me ves, realmente hacen falta y tres productores, o sea, siete personas para hacer la canción de hangar, o sea, siete personas para hacer la canción de hangar, o sea, cuatro letristas para hacer hangar y es que en serio, o sea, me gusta mucho Florens Wax y no quiero hacer nada malo de ella, pero hay una cosa que le pasa un poco a todas estas artistas en meninas que tenemos ahora, es que se rodean de tanto escritor y de tanto productor profesional, es que al final luego acaban convergiendo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Ownership Under Universal
podcast.body: Following EMI's financial restructuring, Abbey Road Studios is now part of Universal. "Now that it's part of Universal, I suppose that it's Universal's property now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parental Split and Blended Family Dynamics
podcast.body: Florence's parents separated, leading to her mother moving in with a new dad who already had three children. This transition shifted Florence from being the eldest child to the middle child in a blended family that "didn't blend so well," causing her to retreat into her bedroom for reading, music, singing, and dancing, finding solace in Billy Holiday's music. "And then her parents split. More serious emotional drama. She, who was a new dad, was a neighbor with three kids of his own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Past Struggles with Alcohol and Sobriety
podcast.body: Florence experienced a period of severe drinking, which contributed to a nervous breakdown between the *Ceremonials* and *How Big, How Blue, How Beautiful* albums. An anecdote includes waking up with a chipped tooth after a night of partying with Kanye West, with no memory of how it happened. She now states that she no longer drinks. "The drinking was pretty severe for a while. After a night of parting with Kanye West, she woke up at the hotel with a chip tooth. No idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personal Adversities and Neurological Conditions
podcast.body: Florence Welch's background includes emotional challenges such as her parents' divorce and the deaths of three grandparents; one died slowly, another, an art historian, committed suicide, and a third, who had encouraged her musical pursuits, died of a stroke. Florence also lives with dyslexia and dyspraxia, a neurological disorder impacting coordination and sometimes short-term memory, which she manages with therapies and which influences her art. "Florence is dyslexic and has something called dyspraxia, which is a neurological disorder that affects the messages the brain gives to other parts of the body when it comes to coordinating movements."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Popularity, Amenities, and Setting
podcast.body: The studio became consistently booked starting around 1979. It was a "gorgeous place" with top-tier gear, a large swimming pool, and a deck offering views of the surrounding mountains and the Soufrière volcano. "It was a gorgeous place, with the best gear, a big swimming pool, and a deck featuring a view of the surrounding mountains and the sufrere volcano off in the distance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Potential Future Buyers
podcast.body: Paul McCartney and Andrew Lloyd Webber have publicly stated their willingness to purchase Abbey Road Studios if it were ever put up for sale again. "And if it were to be put up for sale, people like Paul McCartney and Andrew Lloyd Webber have said that they'd be up for buying it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rebirth as Arts Center
podcast.body: The Château was eventually purchased by four music fans and is now in the process of being reborn as a center for the arts. "Happily, though, it has been purchased by four music fans and is being reborn as a center for the arts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording "Ceremonials" at Abbey Road Studio 1
podcast.body: Florence + The Machine were midway through recording their "Ceremonials" album at Abbey Road Studio 1. Studio 1, despite being the smallest of the Abbey Road studios, was packed with gear for their sessions. "Studio 1, the smallest of the studios, was jammed with gear. Florence and the machine were above midway through recording their ceremonials album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Residential Studio Concept
podcast.body: Following a contemporary trend, AIR Montserrat was designed as a residential studio, allowing musicians to live and work on their projects for as long as needed in an isolated, inspiring environment. "Instruct a state-of-the-art residential facility where musicians could work and play for as long as they liked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Second Location's Transformation into Pulse College
podcast.body: The second location of Windmill Lane in Dublin, previously associated with U2, now operates as Pulse College. This educational institution provides students with training in music production, film music, and video game music. "The second location of Windmill Lane in Dublin, once associated with you too, is now run by Pulse College, where students learn about music production, film music, and video game music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strict Early Etiquette and Schedule
podcast.body: In the studio's early days, producers and engineers were required to wear shirts with collars and ties, even for rock projects. Management also maintained a strict working hour schedule, with a bell ringing at 9 a.m. to mark the start of the workday, a tradition that continues today. "In the old days, producers and engineers were expected to wear shirts with collars and ties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studio One Facilities and Use
podcast.body: Studio One is a massive space, two and a half stories tall, resembling a gigantic gymnasium. It is primarily used for symphonic work and film scores, having hosted a 65-piece orchestra for the final Harry Potter film soundtrack and John Williams' score for *Star Wars*. "Studio One is huge. It's like a gigantic gymnasium, two and a half stories tall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studio One Features and Acoustics
podcast.body: Studio One is equipped with a vintage recording console and features a live room approximately 1200 square feet in size. This room has a very high ceiling, a solid maple floor, and walls constructed from stone and wood, contributing to unique sonic properties that produce recordings unobtainable in a home studio. "It has a vintage recording console and a live room that's about 1200 square feet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studio Three Facilities and Use
podcast.body: Located on the main floor near reception, Studio Three is relatively small and intimate, being only one story tall compared to Studios One and Two. "Studio Three is on the main floor, not too far from reception."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studio Two Facilities and Fame
podcast.body: Studio Two is also quite large, roughly the size of a basketball court with a two-story ceiling. Its control room is on the second floor, overlooking the main recording area. This is the most famous of the studios, where The Beatles conducted all their work. "Studio Two is also quite big. Probably the size of a basketball court, and again, the ceiling is two stories tall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studio Two Notable Clients
podcast.body: Beyond The Beatles, Studio Two has hosted a legendary array of artists, including Pink Floyd, Oasis, Muse, Elbow, Iron Maiden, The Killers, The Hollies, Radiohead, and U2. "Pink Floyd, Oasis, Muse, Elbow, Iron Maiden, The Killers, The Hollies, Radiohead, U2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Subbing for Dave Grohl at Glastonbury
podcast.body: Florence subbed in for Dave Grohl at Glastonbury after he broke his leg falling off a stage in Sweden. This performance highlighted her resilience and ability to step into major roles. "So it's sort of fitting that she subbed in for Dave Grohl at Glastonbury after he broke his leg falling off the stage in Sweden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Success and Artist Retreat
podcast.body: Le Studio achieved great success, allowing artists to "cocoon themselves" for extended periods to complete their projects. Its client list included renowned acts such as Rush, The Police, Sting, The Bee Gees, David Bowie, and Bryan Adams. "La Studio was fantastically successful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Florence Commandments
podcast.body: Isabella Summers attempted to organize Florence's energies by helping her construct a list of guiding principles known as "The Florence Commandments." These ten rules included directives like "always carry seeds," "always carry a book," "dance to all the music, dance hall style," and "climb anything," reflecting Florence's quirky and eccentric approach to life. "There are ten of them. Number one, always carry seeds. Number two, always carry a book. Number three, support your local charity shop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Penthouse Studio
podcast.body: The Penthouse studio, located on the third floor, is exclusively used for mixing and mastering recordings, and is not equipped for setting up instruments or recording. "Then there's the studio up in the third floor called the Penthouse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tony Bongiovi's Background and Vision
podcast.body: Tony Bongiovi began his recording career at 17 at Motown Studios in Detroit, later moving to Media Sound in New York. Observing the rapid changes in recording technology and musical tastes, he conceived a studio design that challenged the conventional "dead" room acoustics of the mid-1970s. "Tony got into the recording game when he was just 17."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touching Equipment During Recording
podcast.body: During a private tour of Abbey Road Studios, an observer admitted to touching a lot of Florence + The Machine's equipment in Studio 1 while they were recording "Ceremonials." The artist later reportedly did not mind this intrusion. "And since some of the big fan of Florence, I kind of touched a lot of her stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Tourist Landmark and Graffiti Tradition
podcast.body: The studio's gate and crosswalk remain a global attraction, drawing fans who frequently stop traffic for photos and write graffiti on the wall alongside the sidewalk. The wall is periodically whitewashed, only for the graffiti to reappear. "That gate in front of the studio, and that crosswalk are still there, and people come from all over the world to stop traffic into right graffiti on the wall that runs along the sidewalk in front of the building."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Twilight Soundtracks Contribution
podcast.body: Florence + The Machine contributed to the various *Twilight* soundtracks that accompanied the film series. These soundtracks featured a nice selection of tunes, mostly album cuts and outtakes, from a range of artists spanning different genres. "The Paramore, Lincoln Park, Collective Soul, Death Cab for Cutie, Tom York, the Killers, Editors, Metric, Block Keys, Dead Weather, Beck, Vampire Weekend, Florence in the Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unconventional Manager Acquisition
podcast.body: Florence Welch secured her current manager, Mayrid Nash, through a highly unusual encounter. While very drunk, Florence pestered Nash, one half of the UK outfit "Queens of Noise," all night before following her into the toilets to sing an "Edgames song." Nash was impressed, and this led to their management deal. "Florence got her current manager when she was very, very drunk. She ran into Mayrid Nash, one half of a UK outfit called Queens of Noise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unique Atmosphere and Host
podcast.body: Magne was known for being an "interesting host," and the studio fostered a decadent atmosphere with frequent parties, abundant alcohol, drugs, and "not infrequent sex parties." "Not only could you live and work at the studio, Manga was also a very interesting host."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unique Design with Glass Windows
podcast.body: The studio was designed with large, floor-to-ceiling glass windows to maximize its connection to the natural environment. While acoustically challenging, this feature was integral to the studio's unique "vibe." "This is why the studio had big floor-deceiling glass windows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Broad Influence on Contemporary Artists
xref.body: Her distinctive style and sound have had a profound impact on a wide range of artists across different genres. Influences can be heard in the music of Florence Welch (Florence + The Machine), Lady Gaga, Lana Del Rey, Alessia Cara, and Billie Eilish. Male singers such as Bruno Mars and Sam Smith also credit Amy as an inspiration. "Her influence can be heard in the music of any number of artists. Florence Welch or Florence in the machine. Lady Gaga, Lana Del Rey, Alissa Carrier and Billie Eilish."
